plates.reference: Own code graphic: on period paper, an inked sensory receptor gene count & combinatorial olfaction chart from Buck & Axel (5 April 1991 Cell 65: 175–187) and Malnic, Hirono, Sato & Buck (5 March 1999 Cell 96: 713–723) contrasts human vision (3 colour cone genes) and taste (~30–40 taste receptor genes across 5 basic tastes) against olfaction (~1,000 receptor genes in mice / ~390–400 functional + ~460 pseudogenes in humans = ~3% of all human genes).

teach_overlay.label: 3 VISION CONE GENES & ~35 TASTE GENES VS ~400 HUMAN (~1,000 MOUSE) OLFACTORY RECEPTOR GENES (~3% OF ENTIRE GENOME)
teach_overlay.detail: Inked human sensory gene allocation & combinatorial receptor chart on period paper comparing 3 colour-vision cone genes and ~35 taste genes against ~400 functional human (~1,000 mammalian) olfactory receptor genes (~3% of the 20,000-gene genome) encoding >10,000 distinct odour chords
teach_overlay.scale: your eyes need just three colour genes to see the entire rainbow — yet your DNA devotes four hundred working genes, or three out of every hundred genes in your body, solely to building smell locks inside your nose

teach_overlay.label: 1-TO-1 LOCK MODEL (400 SMELLS) VS COMBINATORIAL PIANO-CHORD CODE (400 RECEPTORS IN 3–5 KEY CHORDS = BILLIONS OF SCENTS)
teach_overlay.detail: Inked combinatorial chord math chart comparing a 1-to-1 lock-and-key model (400 receptors = only 400 smells) against Buck's combinatorial receptor code (400 receptors taken 3 to 5 at a time = millions to billions of unique receptor chords)
teach_overlay.scale: if each smell receptor recognised only one scent, you could smell only four hundred things — instead, your nose plays those four hundred receptors like chords on a piano, where pressing just four keys at once creates over a billion possible combinations
